DL01.prompt: A network stacks ten affine layers, each a weighted sum plus a bias, with no activation or other nonlinear operation between them. What changes about the set of input-to-output functions it can represent?

options.text: It can represent any curved decision boundary just by adding depth.
options.feedback: Depth alone does not create curvature: composing affine maps still gives an affine map.

options.text: The composition remains affine, although factorization can change optimization or constraints.
options.feedback: Each successive matrix product and bias can be combined into one affine map; the training problem can still change.

options.text: It becomes equivalent to a nearest-neighbour classifier.
options.feedback: Nearest neighbours compare a query with stored examples; stacking affine maps does not introduce that operation.

options.text: It must output zero because the intermediate activations cancel.
options.feedback: Nothing makes the layer outputs cancel. The composite map can have nonzero weights and bias.

DL01.explanation: A hidden nonlinear activation changes the representable function family. Extra affine layers alone do not supply that nonlinearity.

DL01.prompt: A dense network has 3 input features, one hidden layer with 4 units, and 2 output units. Both dense layers have a bias. How many trainable weights and biases are there?

options.feedback: This counts the 12 input-to-hidden and 8 hidden-to-output weights, but misses all six biases.
There are 20 weights and six biases, not four biases. The output layer also has a bias.
The first layer has 3×4+4=16 parameters; the second has 4×2+2=10; total 26.
Batch size does not duplicate stored parameters. Count each shared weight and bias once.

DL01.explanation: Parameter count is input width × output width plus output width for each biased dense layer: 16+10=26.

DL02.prompt: You clear gradients, run the forward pass, calculate a loss, and call loss.backward(). The gradients are finite, but no optimizer step has run. What has happened to the learned weights?

options.text: They have not been updated by backward; an optimizer step is still needed.
options.feedback: Backward computes and accumulates derivatives. Updating parameters is the optimizer's separate job.

options.text: They have moved opposite to the gradient automatically.
options.feedback: Autograd does not apply the learning rate or an optimizer update merely because backward ran.

options.text: They have become equal to their gradients.
options.feedback: Parameter values and their .grad buffers are different state; backward does not replace one with the other.

options.text: They have been reset to their initialization.
options.feedback: Clearing gradients clears derivative buffers, not learned parameter values.

DL02.explanation: A normal loop separates clearing gradients, forward computation, loss, backward, and optimizer.step(). Missing the last operation can produce valid gradients without learning.

DL02.prompt: Let a=w×x, z=a+a, and L=z²/2. At w=2 and x=3, what is dL/dw? Both uses of a belong to the same computation graph.

options.feedback: This is not the derivative of this graph. The output z is 12 and both paths through a contribute.
This includes only one of the two uses of a. Their gradient contributions must be added.
This is dL/dz. You must also multiply through z=2wx to reach w.
z=12, dL/dz=12, and dz/dw=2x=6, so dL/dw=72.

DL02.explanation: Shared intermediate values receive the sum of sensitivities from every downstream path. Here dL/dw=(2wx)×(2x)=72.
DL02.skill: Apply the chain rule across shared paths

DL03.prompt: You freeze all parameters of a pretrained backbone using requires_grad=False, but leave it in training mode. Its BatchNorm layers track running means and variances. Why might its saved state still change?

options.text: requires_grad=False also disables every forward operation.
options.feedback: It prevents parameter gradient computation; it does not prevent the forward pass.

options.text: BatchNorm running statistics are buffers and can still update in training mode.
options.feedback: Freezing learned parameters and freezing mode-dependent running state are different operations.

options.text: The classifier head rewrites the backbone through its output tensor.
options.feedback: A downstream head does not normally rewrite upstream state merely by reading its features.

options.text: BatchNorm always uses exactly the same statistics in training and evaluation.
options.feedback: With tracked statistics, training uses batch information and updates buffers; evaluation normally uses saved statistics.

DL03.explanation: A frozen-feature protocol must specify weights, running state, and train/eval behavior. Disabling parameter gradients alone is not a complete freeze policy.

DL03.prompt: A gradient vector is [6,8]. Before the optimizer transforms it, global L2-norm clipping limits its norm to 2. Ignoring numerical epsilon, which gradient is passed onward?

options.feedback: Norm clipping rescales the whole vector; clipping each coordinate separately would be a different operation.
This vector has norm 1. The requested maximum norm is 2.
The original norm is sqrt(36+64)=10. Multiplying both coordinates by 2/10 gives norm 2.
The original norm exceeds the limit, so a rescaling is required.

DL03.explanation: Global norm clipping preserves this gradient's direction and multiplies its magnitude by 0.2. The subsequent optimizer can transform it further.

DL04.prompt: Training loss keeps falling while development loss rises for several epochs. Your test split has not been inspected. Which action best preserves an honest evaluation?

options.text: Choose the checkpoint with the lowest test loss.
options.feedback: That turns the final test split into selection data and makes its reported score optimistic.

options.text: Report only the lowest training loss.
options.feedback: Training fit does not establish performance on new examples.

options.text: Assume more epochs must eventually fix the development loss.
options.feedback: The pattern is consistent with overfitting; more training is not guaranteed to improve it.

options.text: Use the declared development-based checkpoint rule, and inspect regularization or data issues without selecting on test results.
options.feedback: Development evidence is appropriate for these decisions; the final test remains separate.

DL04.explanation: A widening train/development gap suggests checking overfitting and distribution differences. Checkpoint selection should follow the development rule, not attractive test examples.

DL04.prompt: Five-class label smoothing is defined as target=(1−epsilon)×one_hot+epsilon/5, with epsilon=0.2. What target probability is assigned to the correct class and to each of the four other classes?

options.text: 0.84 for the correct class and 0.04 for each other class.
options.feedback: The correct class receives 0.8+0.04; the others receive 0.04. The probabilities sum to one.

options.text: 0.80 for the correct class and 0.05 for each other class.
options.feedback: That uses a different smoothing convention distributing epsilon only over incorrect classes, not the convention given.

options.text: 1.00 for the correct class and 0.04 for each other class.
options.feedback: This adds probability without reducing the original one-hot target, giving a total larger than one.

options.text: 0.20 for every class.
options.feedback: That is a uniform target and corresponds to epsilon=1 under the stated formula.

DL04.explanation: Always name the smoothing convention. Here the uniform component is added to every class, including the correct class: 0.8+0.2/5=0.84.

DL05.prompt: A convolutional layer applies the same 3×3 filter at every valid image location. What is the main consequence of that weight sharing?

options.text: Its predictions become perfectly invariant to every image translation.
options.feedback: Sharing does not guarantee complete invariance; boundaries, stride, pooling, and the task head still matter.

options.text: It learns a different independent 3×3 filter at each position.
options.feedback: That would remove the sharing assumption and substantially change parameter count.

options.text: It detects a repeated local pattern using the same learned rule across locations.
options.feedback: One filter is reused over spatial patches; this encodes locality and a shared pattern detector.

options.text: It cannot mix information from different input channels.
options.feedback: A standard convolution can mix input channels within each local patch.

DL05.explanation: A convolution reuses local weights instead of learning an unconstrained dense connection at every spatial position. This is an inductive bias, not a promise of universal translation invariance.

DL05.prompt: A biased Conv2d receives a 32×32 image with 3 channels and produces 8 channels. Kernel size is 3×3, stride 2, padding 1, dilation 1, and groups 1. Which output size and parameter count are correct?

options.text: 16×16 spatial output and 224 parameters.
options.feedback: Output length is floor((32+2−2−1)/2+1)=16. Parameters are 8×3×3×3+8=224.

options.text: 32×32 spatial output and 224 parameters.
options.feedback: Padding 1 preserves size at stride 1 for this kernel, not at stride 2.

options.text: 16×16 spatial output and 72 parameters.
options.feedback: 72 counts one input channel's weights and omits both the other channels and eight biases.

options.text: 15×15 spatial output and 216 parameters.
options.feedback: This ignores the stated padding in the size calculation and omits the biases.

DL05.explanation: Spatial output size depends on kernel, padding, stride, and dilation. Stored convolution weights depend on channels, kernel, groups, and bias—not the number of image locations.

DL06.prompt: You compare a plain CNN initialized randomly with a residual CNN that also starts randomly. Which description is supported by that setup?

options.text: It is a clean test of pretrained transfer learning.
options.feedback: Neither model uses pretrained representations, so this is not a transfer-learning comparison.

options.text: It proves that any quality difference comes only from the shortcut.
options.feedback: The residual model can also differ in depth, parameter count, and compute; these need reporting.

options.text: It is a comparison of scratch-trained architectures, with depth, size, and compute differences reported.
options.feedback: Both begin without pretraining. Reporting the changed factors keeps the interpretation appropriately limited.

options.text: It proves residual connections cannot matter unless pretrained weights are used.
options.feedback: Residual connections change computation and gradient paths even when trained from scratch.

DL06.explanation: A residual path and pretrained exposure are different mechanisms. Randomly initialized residual blocks test an architectural design, not reuse of earlier learned representations.
DL06.skill: Separate residual architecture from transfer learning

DL06.prompt: A frozen feature extractor outputs 128 features per image. You train only a new biased linear head for 5 mutually exclusive classes. How many trainable parameters does that head add?

options.feedback: This counts features, not the connections from each feature to each class.
This counts 128×5 weights but omits the five class biases.
A single linear head does not require a second copy of the weight matrix.
The head has 128×5 weights plus 5 biases, totaling 645.

DL06.explanation: Frozen backbone parameters remain stored but are not trainable under this policy. The new head contributes 640 weights and five biases.
DL06.skill: Count trainable parameters in a frozen-feature setup

DL07.prompt: A sequence trainer carries the hidden-state values into the next chunk but detaches that state from the previous computation graph. What does this accomplish?

options.text: It keeps a forward summary but stops gradients from flowing back across the chunk boundary.
options.feedback: Detaching separates stored state values from the earlier derivative history; this is truncated backpropagation through time.

options.text: It resets the hidden state to zero.
options.feedback: Detaching does not reset the state values; explicit reinitialization would do that.

options.text: It allows gradients through every earlier chunk without storing a graph.
options.feedback: The detached boundary removes that gradient connection rather than preserving unlimited history.

options.text: It makes a bidirectional model safe for causal forecasting.
options.feedback: Detaching gradients does not remove future information from a bidirectional forward pass.

DL07.explanation: State carry-over and gradient carry-over are independent choices. A detached state can summarize earlier inputs while bounding backpropagation history and memory.

DL07.prompt: For an illustrative LSTM cell update c_new=f×c_old+i×g, hold the gates fixed at f=0.8 and i=0.25. If c_old=1.5 and the candidate g=0.4, what is c_new?

options.feedback: This treats the old cell as unscaled and does not apply the forget gate.
The retained old content is 0.8×1.5=1.2; new content is 0.25×0.4=0.1; total 1.3.
The two contributions are added, not subtracted.
This is not the stated gated sum. Both retained memory and proposed content contribute.

DL07.explanation: This arithmetic isolates the cell update. It does not by itself calculate the output hidden state or the full network derivative, which also depends on gates and other operations.

DL08.prompt: In next-token training, you stop scoring a future token by masking its loss, but earlier positions can still attend to its input embedding. Has future-information leakage been prevented?

options.text: Yes, because unscored tokens cannot affect the forward pass.
options.feedback: A loss mask changes which outputs are scored, not which inputs attention can read.

options.text: Yes, provided the future token has zero loss weight.
options.feedback: Zero loss weight does not block that token's key or value from attention.

options.text: No; removing future tokens from the loss also requires deleting all positional information.
options.feedback: Position information and visibility are separate; a causal attention mask can preserve positions while blocking future access.

options.text: No; a causal attention mask must separately block unavailable future keys before attention normalization.
options.feedback: Loss masking and information-flow masking perform different jobs and need separate tests.

DL08.explanation: Earlier representations can exploit unscored future inputs unless the attention visibility rule excludes them. Test causality by changing future inputs and checking earlier outputs.
DL08.skill: Distinguish attention masks from loss masks

DL08.prompt: One attention row has scores [ln(3),0,−infinity] after scaling and masking. The corresponding scalar values are [4,8,100]. What is its weighted output after softmax?

options.feedback: An equal average ignores both the unequal scores and the masked third position.
Exponentiated scores are [3,1,0], so weights are [0.75,0.25,0] and output is 0.75×4+0.25×8=5.
Attention takes a normalized weighted sum, not the sum of the two unmasked values.
The third value has zero attention weight because its score is masked.

DL08.explanation: Softmax normalizes over permitted keys. A large masked value contributes nothing, and attention weights are mixing coefficients rather than probabilities that statements are true.

DL09.prompt: On the same held-out inputs and with reconstruction error measured in the same original units, an autoencoder has lower error than PCA. You have not tested a classifier or retrieval task on either representation. What can you conclude?

options.text: The autoencoder is now proven better for classification.
options.feedback: Reconstructing pixels and preserving class-relevant information are different objectives.

options.text: The autoencoder has learned only human-readable factors.
options.feedback: Reconstruction loss does not establish that its latent features correspond to interpretable factors.

options.text: It reconstructed better under the stated evaluation; downstream usefulness still needs a separate test.
options.feedback: A fixed downstream probe or controlled fine-tuning comparison can test utility beyond reconstruction.

options.text: PCA must have been fitted incorrectly.
options.feedback: A more flexible reconstruction model can outperform a linear reference without implying an implementation error.

DL09.explanation: Report the measured task honestly. Lower reconstruction error supports a reconstruction claim, not an unmeasured transfer, class-prediction, or retrieval claim.
DL09.skill: Separate representation training loss from downstream utility

DL09.prompt: An input vector is [1,0,1] and its reconstruction is [0.5,0.2,0.9]. Using the mean of the three squared coordinate errors, what is reconstruction MSE?

options.feedback: Squared errors are 0.25, 0.04, and 0.01. Their sum is 0.30; dividing by three gives 0.10.
This is the sum of squared errors, not their mean over three coordinates.
This is the mean absolute error: (0.5+0.2+0.1)/3. MSE squares errors first.
This includes only the third coordinate and omits the other two errors.

DL09.explanation: State the reduction: mean squared error averages squared differences over the declared coordinates. A different reduction would change the scalar and its gradient scale.
DL09.skill: Calculate reconstruction error with an explicit reduction

DL10.prompt: A GAN discriminator becomes very accurate at separating real from generated images. What is the most defensible interpretation by itself?

options.text: The generator must be producing excellent images.
options.feedback: A discriminator can be accurate precisely because generated examples are easy to distinguish.

options.text: The generator has definitely memorized all training images.
options.feedback: Discriminator accuracy alone does not identify memorization; that needs separate evidence.

options.text: The generator must be diverse because two networks were trained.
options.feedback: Two-network training does not prevent mode collapse or establish diversity.

options.text: The discriminator currently separates the two sources; generator quality, diversity, and memorization need separate checks.
options.feedback: One adversarial component's success is not a standalone certificate of the generator's quality.

DL10.explanation: GAN objectives are coupled. Inspect generated samples under a fixed rule and use appropriate held-out quality, diversity, and memorization checks rather than treating discriminator accuracy as a universal score.

DL10.prompt: A stated beta-VAE objective is reconstruction cost + beta×KL. For one example, reconstruction cost is 7 nats, KL is 0.5 nats, and beta=3. What is that objective?

options.text: 7.5 nats
options.feedback: This would use beta=1 and ignores the specified multiplier of three.

options.text: 8.5 nats
options.feedback: 7+3×0.5=8.5. The KL weighting changes the objective; it is not a direct measurement of visual sharpness.

options.text: 22.5 nats
options.feedback: This incorrectly multiplies the reconstruction term by beta as well.

options.text: 6.5 nats
options.feedback: The stated minimized cost adds the weighted KL term; it does not subtract it.

DL10.explanation: The arithmetic is 7+1.5=8.5 nats. Changing beta changes the trade-off, so arbitrary beta values should not be described as the unchanged original negative-ELBO objective.
DL10.skill: Calculate and interpret a weighted latent-model objective

DL11.prompt: In a declared transductive node-classification experiment, the full graph and test-node features are available during training, but test labels are withheld. Which addition would cross that information boundary?

options.text: Using permitted unlabelled test-node features in message passing.
options.feedback: That access is allowed by the stated transductive protocol, although it would need a different description in an inductive task.

options.text: Recording whether evaluation uses one known graph or unseen graphs.
options.feedback: This clarifies the access policy; it does not leak a target.

options.text: Appending the withheld test-node label to each test node's input features.
options.feedback: This supplies the answer as an input and invalidates the intended held-out label evaluation.

options.text: Comparing with an MLP using the same permitted node attributes.
options.feedback: This is a useful reference for separating attribute information from relational information.

DL11.explanation: Transductive access does not mean unrestricted access. Permitted graph structure and unlabelled attributes are different from the targets being evaluated.
DL11.skill: Audit graph access and label leakage

DL11.prompt: A toy message-passing layer averages a node's own vector [3,0] with its two neighbours [0,3] and [6,3]. There are no learned transformations, and all weights are equal. What is the aggregate?

options.feedback: This averages the neighbours alone, omitting the self vector that the prompt explicitly includes.
This is the component-wise sum, not the mean over three vectors.
The first components sum to nine, not three, before division.
The component-wise sum is [9,6]; dividing by three included vectors gives [3,2].

DL11.explanation: The self-inclusion and aggregation rule matter. This equal-weight mean is a toy rule, not automatically the degree-normalized update used by every graph architecture.

DL12.prompt: An image can contain both a bicycle and a pedestrian. You need one presence score for each label, and both labels may be true. Which output/loss design fits that target?

options.text: Two independent logits trained with a binary loss for each label.
options.feedback: Multilabel targets allow multiple positive indicators, unlike mutually exclusive softmax classes.

options.text: One two-class softmax that forces exactly one label per image.
options.feedback: A softmax competition would incorrectly force the two labels to exclude one another.

options.text: A single number interpreted as the coordinates of both objects.
options.feedback: Object presence and localization are different targets; one scalar cannot encode both stated presence indicators.

options.text: A per-pixel segmentation mask, because all image tasks require one.
options.feedback: Segmentation needs spatial annotations and answers a different question from image-level presence.

DL12.explanation: Start from target meaning: several labels can be present, so the outputs should not be forced to sum to one. Localization or segmentation would require additional targets and heads.
DL12.skill: Match a task head and loss to label semantics

DL12.prompt: A predicted foreground region contains 8 pixels, the reference region contains 6 pixels, and their intersection contains 4 pixels. What is intersection-over-union (IoU)?

options.feedback: 4/8 is precision for this foreground prediction, not intersection divided by union.
Union size is 8+6−4=10, so IoU=4/10=0.40.
4/6 is recall against the reference foreground, not IoU.
2×4/(8+6) is Dice overlap, a different metric from IoU.

DL12.explanation: Subtract the intersection once when forming the union to avoid counting shared pixels twice. Naming the metric matters because precision, recall, Dice, and IoU use different denominators.

DL13.prompt: You save only model weights and later want to reproduce the exact next training update from an interrupted Adam run. What is missing from the continuation contract?

options.text: Nothing; weights fully determine the next update for every training setup.
options.feedback: The next data batch, optimizer moments, schedules, and randomness can all affect continuation.

options.text: Only the final test score.
options.feedback: A test score does not restore the training computation or its state.

options.text: A screenshot of the learning curve.
options.feedback: A chart records observations, not optimizer buffers or sampler position.

options.text: Optimizer and scheduler state, random-generator state, data position, and compatible settings as applicable.
options.feedback: These states can change the next gradient or update even when the starting weights match.

DL13.explanation: An inference weights file and a resumable training checkpoint serve different purposes. Exact continuation needs the relevant state and a tested restoration procedure under stated numerical tolerances.

DL13.prompt: You accumulate gradients over two microbatches using per-example mean losses. The first has 6 examples with mean loss 2; the second has 2 examples with mean loss 6. What combined mean matches one batch of all 8 examples?

options.feedback: The weighted mean is (6×2+2×6)/8=24/8=3; each example receives equal weight.
An unweighted average of the two means overweights each example in the smaller microbatch.
Adding batch means does not account for either their sizes or the total example count.
This is the total loss sum over the examples, not the requested per-example mean.

DL13.explanation: Unequal microbatches need size-aware weighting. Averaging their means is equivalent only when their included example counts are equal under the stated objective.

DL14.prompt: A pretrained CNN beats a scratch linear classifier after much more tuning. Both use the same final test split. What claim can this comparison support without further controls?

options.text: The CNN architecture alone caused the entire gain.
options.feedback: Architecture, prior data exposure, and selection budget changed together; their individual effects are not identified.

options.text: Pretraining and tuning budget are irrelevant because the test set matches.
options.feedback: Matching the test set does not remove differences in starting information or model-selection work.

options.text: The selected CNN system performed better under those stated conditions; an architecture-only claim needs additional controls.
options.feedback: This reports the result while keeping prior exposure and tuning differences visible.

options.text: The result must be discarded because models can never have different resources.
options.feedback: Different-resource comparisons can be informative when their question and limitations are clearly stated.

DL14.explanation: Fairness depends on the question. A system-quality comparison can allow different resources, but it should not be presented as a controlled test of architecture alone.
DL14.skill: Keep comparison claims within the tested controls

DL14.prompt: A dataset has exactly 1,000 training examples. With batch size 128, no dropped cases, no gradient accumulation, and one optimizer update per batch, how many updates occur over 3 complete epochs?

options.text: 21 updates, because every batch must contain 128 examples.
options.feedback: This drops the final partial batch even though the prompt explicitly retains all cases.

options.text: 24 updates, with 104 examples in each epoch's final batch.
options.feedback: Seven full batches contain 896 examples; the remaining 104 form batch eight. Three epochs give 3×8=24 updates.

options.text: 3 updates, one per epoch.
options.feedback: An epoch contains several batches; the prompt specifies one update per batch.

options.text: 384 updates, because batch size times epochs determines update count.
options.feedback: 128×3 counts neither batches nor optimizer steps. Update count depends on dataset size divided into batches.

DL14.explanation: Use ceil(1,000/128)=8 batches per epoch when retaining the last partial batch. Epochs, updates, and processed examples are different accounting units.
